newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's CDU and SPD see chance for tax deal.
newsitem.headline: Germany's CDU and SPD see chance for tax deal.

text.p: Leading members of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) held out hope on Saturday that they could reach a compromise over sweeping reforms to the German tax system.

CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said he thought Kohl's ruling coalition and the SPD would reach an agreement in a parliamentary committee due to discuss a government tax bill, despite the failure of talks between the two sides last week.
"The Social Democrats will not keep up their stubborn attitude. We will come to an agreement in the committee," Hintze told the Magdeburger Volksstimme daily.

SPD chief whip Peter Struck agreed a compromise was possible but said Finance Minister Theo Waigel would have to drop some aspects of the bill -- aimed at cutting taxes by 30 billion marks ($17.4 billion) over the next two years -- to win the SPD's agreement.

"Finance Minister Waigel will have to take stock. If he is ready to drop things, like the taxation of supplementary pay for shift work, that we definitely cannot accept, then I think a compromise is possible," Struck told Berlin radio.
The bill, facing the obstacle of an SPD-led Bundesrat upper house of parliament, is likely to go before the lower house committee before parliament starts its summer break in July.

Struck denied that the SPD was divided over the issue of cutting the top rate of income tax, currently 53 percent. "There are no differences of opinion between (SPD leader) Oskar Lafontaine, the state premiers and the parliamentary party," he said.

Struck said the party's position on the issue had not changed since the beginning of negotiations with the government. The SPD would only back cuts to top income tax rates if they were paid for through offsetting measures.

Lafontaine, who had tried to enforce a party line blocking any "tax giveaways for the rich", changed his position on the top rate of tax on Monday after powerful SPD figures -- including rival Gerhard Schroeder -- backed compromise.

In a release ahead of publication on Sunday, Welt am Sonntag newspaper said Schroeder, Lafontaine's main challenger to be the SPD's candidate for chancellor at the general election in October 1998, argued that states had a "constitutional duty" to agree to the government's reforms.

Still unclear is how far the SPD would be prepared to go towards Waigel's plan to cut the top rate of income tax to 39 percent in 1999, although media reports say SPD regional leaders would be ready to see a top rate of 46 percent.
Wolfgang Schaueble, the powerful parliamentary leader of the CDU, said SPD regional leaders had a duty to back reform.
"If the SPD-led state parliaments take seriously their responsibility for job-seekers, they cannot refuse to consent to this tax reform," Schaueble told the Nordsee Zeitung daily.
Schaueble said the CDU would continue parliamentary proceedings to push through the tax reform bill before the summer recess.

Hintze said the cornerstones of the reform plan were non-negotiable, including the lowering of across-the-board tax rates, the removal of some tax deductions and a net lowering of the tax burden, but said the goverment was prepared to compromise on other components.
Hintze also called on Lafontaine to compromise over pension reform. "I really hope that Herr Lafontaine will not extend his blockage to pensions," he said.
Struck said the SPD did not rule out chances of a deal, but would not agree to plans by Labour Minister Norbert Bluem to cut pension levels to 64 percent of salary.
